1.1a — Launch: Fork, Clone & Press Play

Today you get the game you will be building for the next four months. It already works — that is the point. You fork it, clone it, press Play, and see every system you will learn to build this semester: movement, coins, spikes, a turret, an enemy. Then all year you will take it apart and rebuild every piece as your own.

Setup Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — Fork the starter. Log into GitHub, open the cs-curriculum-main repo your teacher links in Canvas, and click Fork (top right). A fork is a copy of the repo that belongs to you — your commits go to your copy, and you can never break the original.

Fork vs. clone — say it out loud: fork copies the repo on GitHub (server to server, yours forever). Clone downloads a repo to this machine (server to laptop). You do both today: fork first, then clone your fork.

Step 2 — Clone your fork. On your fork's page click the green Code button, copy the HTTPS URL, then in GitHub Desktop: File → Clone Repository → URL tab → paste → Clone. Or if you use the terminal: 

git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/cs-curriculum-main.git

Step 3 — Open it in Unity. Open Unity Hub → Add → pick your cloned cs-curriculum-main folder. The first open takes a while (it imports every sprite in the game). When it finishes, you should see three scenes in Assets/_Scenes: Start, Overworld, and Platformer.

Step 4 — Press Play. Open the Start scene and hit the Play button. Then open the Overworld scene and press Play again — walk with WASD or the arrow keys, collect a coin, touch a spike, walk near the turret, get chased by the enemy. Watch the Console tab while you do it.

Tinker: The Console is your window into the game

While playing the Overworld, collect a coin and watch the Console (Window → General → Console if it is not open). Then touch a spike. What two different things print, and how do the numbers change each time you repeat the action?

Tour ~15 min

What is actually in this repo? Find each of these in the Project window — you will touch all of them this year:

FolderWhat lives thereYour first date with it
Assets/_ScenesStart, Overworld, Platformer — the three levelsToday
Assets/ScriptsThe C# you will rewrite: PlayerController, StatManager, TurretController, EnemyController, LeverLesson 1.3
Assets/PrefabsReady-made game objects: Coin, Spikes, Turret, Player, projectiles, the axe, the switchUnit 2
Assets/ArtworkTop-down grass and walls; cave and entrance tiles for the platformerUnit 7
Assets/AnimationsThe player animator with axe and shovel variantsLesson 1.6

The scene split matters all year: the same PlayerController.cs runs in every scene — but when the scene is Platformer it switches to jumping physics and gravity. One script, two games. You will find that if statement in Unit 5 and add to it in Unit 6.

Socratic

This starter is on GitHub, public, with an open license — you copied it and you will build a product on it, legally. Why is that allowed, and what does the license obligate you to do? (We settle this question for real in 9.10a — but take a guess now.)

Ship It ~10 min

Commit — the habit that starts today. In GitHub Desktop (or git add / git commit -m / git push), commit with the message "1.1a: cloned the starter" and push. From now on: every single class ends with a commit and a push. Your commit history is the receipt of your whole year.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain the difference between a fork and a clone
  • Open any scene in Unity and press Play
  • Find the Console tab and read a Debug.Log line
  • Name the three scenes and what makes the Platformer one different
  • Commit and push to your own fork
